summary: First English narrative for Reed Hastings' September 2011 decision to split Netflix's DVD service into a separate Qwikster brand and website, written from the case's verified facts (Netflix SEC-filed shareholder letters of July, September and October 2011 and January 2012; contemporary reports quoting the 18 September and 10 October announcements).

narrative.hook: Your customers are furious about a price increase that is only now reaching their bills, and you have just told investors to expect fewer subscribers. You believe DVD-by-mail is the past and streaming the future. Do you finish the break-up now, with a new name and a new website for DVDs, or leave customers with the one Netflix account they know?
narrative.short_setup: It is September 2011, and Reed Hastings runs Netflix. In July the company split its U.S. service into two plans, $7.99 a month for unlimited streaming and $7.99 for unlimited DVDs by mail. For people who used both, the bill went from $9.99 to $15.98, an increase Netflix itself put at as much as 60%, taking effect when each member renewed in September. Netflix also set up a dedicated DVD division and said it had no intention of selling it. By its own July estimate, about 12 million Americans subscribed to both services. On 15 September the company lowered its domestic subscriber estimates for the quarter, acknowledging that the split had upset many subscribers while insisting it was the right long-term choice. Hastings is now weighing the next step: whether to give the DVD business its own brand, website, account and bill.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: The case for a clean break starts with where the business was heading. Netflix had said DVD shipments had likely peaked, and streaming was where it saw its future. Hastings' stated fear was that most companies that are great at one thing, like AOL with dial-up or Borders with bookstores, never become great at the next thing people want. A separate DVD company with its own name and website would let the streaming service change faster without carrying the DVD business in its design and marketing, and would give DVD an identity of its own, with room for additions such as video game rentals. The price change had already done the damage of separating the two; finishing the job quickly could be better than prolonging it.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: The case for keeping one account is about timing and the customer. The price increase was only just reaching members' bills, the company had just cut its subscriber estimates, and about 12 million people used both services. For them a second website meant two queues, two accounts and two charges, at the moment they were most annoyed. The organisational separation the strategy needed already existed: Netflix had created a dedicated DVD division in July and had said that was the best way to run DVD. Keeping the separate prices but one website would let the anger settle before asking customers to change anything else.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: Hastings chose the clean break. On 18 September 2011 he published a post that began 'I messed up', apologised that members felt the company lacked respect and humility in how it had announced the separation, and then announced that the DVD service would be renamed Qwikster. It would have its own website, its own queue and ratings, a separate charge, and video game rentals for an extra fee. As reported at the time, the post said the Qwikster.com and Netflix.com websites would not be integrated, so a change of e-mail address or credit card would have to be made in both places. Answering readers' comments, Hastings argued that separate websites would let the company improve both faster. His stated reason for the whole move was the fear of failing to make the leap from DVDs to streaming.
narrative.outcome_story: The reaction was hostile, and three weeks later Netflix gave up. On 10 October Hastings wrote that two websites would make things more difficult for members: there would be 'one website, one account, one password… in other words, no Qwikster.' The separate prices stayed. On 24 October Netflix reported that its unique U.S. subscribers had fallen from 24.59 million to 23.79 million in the quarter, and described the 'PR storm that engulfed our brand'. Its own diagnosis was that the price change was the main problem and that the announced-and-retracted DVD brand, while it caused a temporary surge in cancellations, had a relatively minor impact by comparison. In the next quarter DVD subscriptions fell by 2.76 million to 11.17 million, while streaming subscriptions grew by 220,000 to 21.67 million, with December additions ahead of forecast.
narrative.hindsight_analysis:
It is easy to read Qwikster as a fiasco and stop there. The decision and its result need to be looked at separately.

On decision quality, this case rates the choice as weak, though the rating is contestable. The strategic idea behind it was serious: DVD was in decline, streaming was the future, and Hastings' worry about incumbents failing to adapt was a real risk for any company in Netflix's position. But almost everything known at the time argued against doing it then. Customers were already angry. The price change was only now arriving on their bills, and the company had just lowered its subscriber estimates. About 12 million people would bear the cost of a second site and account. Meanwhile the internal separation the strategy needed was already in place, in a DVD division Netflix had itself called the best way to run that business. The new brand added customer friction without adding much that the company did not already have.

On outcome quality, the result was bad: a public reversal within three weeks, and damage to trust that Netflix itself acknowledged. But the size of that damage is uncertain. Netflix's own account says most of the subscriber loss came from the price change, and the two effects overlapped in time, so no one can neatly separate them. That account is the company's view, not an independent measurement. The quick reversal also limited the cost. Nor does the later growth of streaming prove the decision right or wrong; the company stayed on its streaming course whether or not Qwikster existed.

The fair verdict is a sound strategy attached to a poorly timed move. The direction was defensible. The decision to impose a second change on angry customers, for a separation that already existed inside the company, was the weak part.
narrative.decision_principle: A strategy can be right while a step taken in its name is wrong: before adding friction for customers, ask whether the step buys anything you do not already have, and whether this is the moment they can absorb it.
narrative.longform_story:
In the summer of 2011, Netflix was two businesses wearing one name. One was the business that had made it famous: DVDs rented by mail. The other was streaming, which Netflix had come to see as its future. In July the company made that split visible in its prices. Streaming and DVDs became two separate plans at $7.99 a month each. Members who wanted both now paid $15.98 instead of $9.99, an increase the company itself said could reach 60%. The change took effect when each member renewed in September.

Netflix explained the move to investors in its July letter. Streaming was growing fast, and DVD shipments had likely peaked. The company set up a dedicated DVD division under a long-serving executive and said it could best run DVD by mail as a division, adding that it had no intention of selling it. It estimated that by the end of September it would have about 22 million streaming subscribers and 15 million DVD subscribers in the United States, and that about 12 million people would be subscribing to both.

The customers who used both did not take the price change quietly. On 15 September Netflix lowered its domestic subscriber estimates for the quarter. 'We know our decision to split our services has upset many of our subscribers,' the letter said, 'which we don't take lightly.' The company remained convinced, it said, that the split was the right long-term choice. It would allow a dedicated DVD division, faster improvement of the global streaming service, more spending on streaming content, and low prices.

This is where Reed Hastings had to decide what to do next. One path was to finish what July had started. The DVD business could get its own name, its own website and its own billing, leaving Netflix free to be a streaming company. Hastings' worry, which he would soon put in writing, was the classic fate of incumbents. Most companies that are great at something, he wrote, like AOL with dial-up or Borders with bookstores, do not become great at the new things people want. For Netflix the new thing was streaming. A clean separation would let the streaming side move without the DVD business in its way.

The other path was to hold still. The prices were already separate, and the DVD division already existed. The price increase was only now arriving on customers' bills, and anger was at its peak. Adding a second website and a second account would hit hardest exactly the people already most upset: the roughly 12 million who used both services. The strategy did not obviously require a new brand. Waiting would cost some speed, but would avoid asking customers to absorb two shocks in one season.

On 18 September 2011 Hastings chose the first path. His post opened with an apology: 'I messed up.' He wrote that many members felt Netflix had lacked respect and humility in the way it announced the separation, and he apologised for that. Then he explained what came next. The DVD service would be renamed Qwikster. It would have its own website, with its own queue and ratings, and a separate charge on members' statements. It would add video game rentals for an extra fee. As reported at the time, the post said the two websites would not be integrated. A member who changed an e-mail address or credit card would have to do it twice. When readers objected in the comments, Hastings replied that separate websites would let the company improve both faster.

The apology was meant to calm customers. The announcement that followed it did the opposite. On 10 October, three weeks later, Netflix backed down. Hastings wrote that two websites would make things more difficult for members, so Netflix would keep 'one website, one account, one password… in other words, no Qwikster.' The separate prices stayed; the company said it was done with price changes.

The quarter's numbers came on 24 October. Unique U.S. subscribers had fallen from 24.59 million to 23.79 million. Netflix described a 'PR storm that engulfed our brand' and admitted it had hurt its hard-earned reputation. But its own account of the damage gave Qwikster a smaller role than popular memory does. The main problem, the company wrote, was the price change, and what it had misjudged was how quickly to move. The announced-and-retracted DVD brand had further dented its reputation and caused a temporary surge of cancellations, but compared with the price change its impact was relatively minor.

The longer story went on as Netflix had intended. In the last quarter of 2011, DVD subscriptions fell by 2.76 million to 11.17 million, while streaming subscriptions grew by 220,000 to 21.67 million, with December ahead of the company's forecast. The streaming strategy continued with or without a separate DVD brand.

It is tempting to tell this as the story of a visionary who was right about streaming and wrong about everything else, or of a chief executive who simply blundered. Neither quite fits. The direction was reasonable, and the fear behind it was real. But the move made in its name asked angry customers to accept a second change, for a separation the company had already achieved inside its own walls. How much it actually cost is hard to measure, because the price change was hurting at the same time and Netflix's estimate of the split is its own. What is clear is that a good destination did not make the timing of this particular step a good decision.
